newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile summit to debate democracy and dictatorship.
newsitem.headline: Chile summit to debate democracy and dictatorship.

text.p: The leaders of 19 Latin American countries plus Spain and Portugal gather in Chile on Saturday for an Ibero-American summit whose official theme is how to get Latin Americans to care about democracy.

Chilean President Eduardo Frei will host the meeting of high-profile leaders such as Cuba's Fidel Castro and Brazil's Fernando Henrique Cardoso, as well as the prime ministers of Spain and Portugal, both making their first appearance at a summit of this kind.
The official theme of the summit -- "Governability in an Efficient and Participative Democracy" -- may sound more like an issue for a sociologists' convention than for a meeting of presidents.

But Chilean officials, who picked the theme, insist it has relevance in a region where millions of people live under elected governments but do not bother to vote, do not care about politics and may not even care if they live under dictatorship or democracy.

"What does governability mean? It means building a better, more participative government, within reach of its citizens ... That's what we are going to have a rich and profound dialogue about,'' Frei said in a speech on Friday.

The theme separates this summit from the five previous Ibero-American meetings, which began in Guadalajara, Mexico, in 1990 as a way of forging closer ties between Latin America and its former colonial masters Spain and Portugal.

"Generally at these summits, people talk about economic and social development. This is the first summit of any kind in which we'll be talking about political development," said the summit's chief organiser, Fabio Vio.
"Looking at concrete issues, for example, there is an alarming trend among young people not bothering to vote. Trends like that are dangerous for democracy,'' Vio told Reuters.

Most of Latin America returned to democratic rule in the 1980s after long spells of dictatorship, in processes that resembled the transitions to democracy in Spain and Portugal in the 1970s. Chile was among the last, restoring civilian rule only in 1990.

But a poll conducted throughout Latin America last month showed more than a third of Latin Americans either openly supported the return of authoritarian rule or were indifferent as to whether they lived in a democracy or not.

The poll showed that 17 percent of Latin Americans would support a return to dicatorship and 17 percent said they did not care what form of government they lived under. The numbers contrasted sharply with Spain, where only seven percent said they wanted a return to dictatorship.

How the summit will translate three days of talk into action has yet to be answered by the presidents, who will officially open the summit at a Santiago convention centre on Sunday and then move to the seaside city of Vina del Mar for a final day of talks on Monday.
All the leaders arrive on Saturday, except those of five Central American countries and the Dominican Republic who flew into Santiago on Friday night.

There is also the question of how to approach the one leader at the summit who was not elected -- Castro, who has held firm against changes to Cuba's one-party system and promises to be the centre of media attention at the summit.

Diplomats said the summit's final document was unlikely to make any call for democratic reforms or respect for human rights at all in Cuba, despite efforts by Spain's delegation for some kind of reference.
But the document is sure to include a strongly-worded condemnation of the Helms-Burton Act tightening the U.S. embargo on Cuba, diplomats said.
